name: Pazhampathinathar Temple, Tiruppunavasal
deity: Shiva as Pazhampathinathar (Viruthapureeswarar), with the goddess Periyanayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Pandya coast, sung in the Tevaram (7th to 8th century); the present structure reflects later Pandya and Chola-influenced building
dynasty: Pandya (later construction credited to a Sundara Pandya)
summary: Pazhampathinathar, the Lord of the Ancient Town, is worshipped at Tiruppunavasal on the Pandya coast, the Tiruppunavayil of Sambandar's and Sundarar's hymns, a shrine known for a linga and pedestal said to be of unusually great girth.

sections.history: Tiruppunavasal, the Tiruppunavayil of the Tevaram, is a coastal village in Avudaiyarkoil taluk of Pudukkottai district. The temple is one of the fourteen Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Pandya country, and the hymns of both Sambandar and Sundarar praise it. Its name is read as the entrance of the river and the sea, for the village lies where the water meets the shore. Tradition calls the place by many names across the ages, from Vajravanam and Indrapuram to Brahmapuram and Vriddha Kasi, the older Kasi, and in the present age Vriddhapuri and Pazhampathi; the Tamil name Pazhampathinathar and the Sanskrit Viruthapureeswarar both carry the sense of the Lord of the ancient town. A Pandya inscription of the fifteenth regnal year of Vikrama Pandya records a land gift for worship and upkeep, and later construction is credited to a Sundara Pandya, in a blend of Pandya and Chola manner.
sections.architecture: The temple's rajagopuram is about sixty-five feet tall, and the style of the later construction is described as a blend of Pandya and Chola. The pride of the sanctum is the Shiva linga and its pedestal, the avudaiyar, said to have the largest circumference of any in Tamil Nadu, which gives the Lord here a notable breadth and presence. The goddess Periyanayaki is worshipped in her own east-facing shrine. The temple's sacred water is the Brahma Theertham, said to have been made by Brahma himself. We have not found a detailed account of the mandapas, tiers or sculptural programme, so only these features are described.
sections.legends: Two accounts are told of this place. In the sthala purana, Brahma lost his office as Creator because he could not explain the meaning of the Pranava mantra, and on the advice of Parvati he came to earth, installed a Shiva linga here and worshipped it until his position was restored; the tank he made for the Lord's abhishekam is the Brahma Theertham. In another telling, Indra worshipped here to be freed from the curse of the sage Gautama. Local belief also holds that Yama and his messengers cannot enter the boundary of Tiruppunavasal, which makes the village a place of fearless devotion. Sources differ on details, and we have kept to the accounts most widely repeated.
sections.festivals: The major festival is the eleven-day Vaikasi Visakam, held in the Tamil month of Vaikasi (May to June), when the temple is celebrated with great splendour. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruppunavasal is a quiet coastal village, and the temple suits those who like to arrive without haste. Come first to the sanctum of Pazhampathinathar and take in the breadth of the linga and its great pedestal, then visit the goddess Periyanayaki in her own shrine, and walk on to the Brahma Theertham. The sea air and the open sky give the visit a calm of their own. Traffic in the village is light and the temple tends to close early, so plan to arrive in good time before the midday and evening closings. Many pilgrims pair the visit with Tiruvadanai, another Tevaram shrine about 21 km away.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6:00 am to 11:30 am and again from about 4:00 or 5:00 pm to about 7:30 pm (one listing runs to 8:30 pm); the temple tends to close early, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruppunavasal is a coastal village in Avudaiyarkoil taluk, Pudukkottai district, about 25 km south of Avudaiyarkoil and reached from there by road. Tiruvadanai, another Paadal Petra Sthalam, lies about 21 km away. Rail and air connections are not confirmed in our sources, so plan the last stretch by road and confirm bus services locally. Traffic in the village is light.
